title: Τηλεμάχου ἀγγελία καὶ ὁδὸς εἰς ἄστυ
titleEn: Telemachus's Report and the Road to Town — Odyssey 17.101–203
part: Telemachus's Report and the Road to Town (17.101–203)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Penelope says that she will go up to rest, and asks why her son has told her nothing of his father. Telemachus tells what Nestor said, and what Menelaus told him of Proteus: Odysseus is alive on Calypso's island and cannot get home. The seer Theoclymenus swears that Odysseus is already in Ithaca, and Penelope hopes he is right. Out in the court the suitors are at their games until Medon calls them in to dinner. Odysseus and Eumaeus set out for the town together, the swineherd uneasy at leaving the farm and Odysseus dressed as a beggar with wallet and staff.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἦ τοι ἐγὼν ὑπερώϊον εἰσαναβᾶσα
λέξομαι εἰς εὐνήν, ἥ μοι στονόεσσα τέτυκται,
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, ē toi egōn hyperōïon eisanabasa
lexomai eis eunēn, hē moi stonoessa tetyktai,
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, I for my part, to the upper room having gone up,
will lie down in bed, which to me groan-filled has been made,
sentences.i: “Telemachus, I am going up to the upper room to lie down in my bed, which has become groan-filled for me,
sentences.n: Penelope's speech begins here; the previous part closed with its introductory line (17.100). Τηλέμαχ’ is the vocative with its final vowel elided. ἐγών is the Homeric form of ἐγώ. εἰσαναβᾶσα is the aorist participle of εἰσαναβαίνω 'go up into'. λέξομαι is a future middle, 'I will lie down'. ἥ is the relative 'which', agreeing with εὐνήν. στονόεσσα 'groan-filled' is built on στόνος 'groan', and τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω 'make', so 'has been made' or 'has become'.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ δάκρυσ’ ἐμοῖσι πεφυρμένη, ἐξ οὗ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ᾤχεθ’ ἅμ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν ἐς Ἴλιον·
sentences.tr:
aiei dakrys’ emoisi pephyrmenē, ex hou Odysseus
ōicheth’ ham’ Atreïdēisin es Ilion·
sentences.l:
ever with my tears mingled, since Odysseus
went off with the sons of Atreus to Ilium;
sentences.i: always soaked with my tears, ever since Odysseus went off with the sons of Atreus to Ilium;
sentences.n: αἰεί is the Homeric form of ἀεί 'always'. πεφυρμένη is the perfect passive participle of φύρω 'mix, soak', feminine because it agrees with εὐνή, the bed of the previous unit; δάκρυσ’ is the dative plural δάκρυσι with its vowel elided. ἐξ οὗ is 'from the time when'. ᾤχεθ’ is ᾤχετο, imperfect of οἴχομαι 'be gone, go off'. Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, 'with the sons of Atreus' (Agamemnon and Menelaus). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μοι ἔτλης,
πρὶν ἐλθεῖν μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας ἐς τόδε δῶμα,
νόστον σοῦ πατρὸς σάφα εἰπέμεν, εἴ που ἄκουσας.
sentences.tr:
oude moi etlēs,
prin elthein mnēstēras agēnoras es tode dōma,
noston sou patros sapha eipemen, ei pou akousas.
sentences.l:
and not to me did you bring yourself,
before the lordly suitors came to this house,
of your father's homecoming clearly to tell, if anywhere you heard.”
sentences.i: and you did not bring yourself to tell me plainly, before the lordly suitors came to this house, of your father's homecoming, if you had heard anything anywhere.”
sentences.n: ἔτλης is the aorist of τλάω 'endure, bring oneself to', here with an infinitive, 'you could bring yourself to'. πρὶν ἐλθεῖν 'before they came' takes the infinitive, as πρίν often does. μνηστῆρας ἀγήνορας is the standing 'lordly suitors'. νόστον is the object of the infinitive εἰπέμεν (= εἰπεῖν) and σοῦ πατρὸς is 'of your father'. σάφα 'clearly' is an adverb, and εἴ που ἄκουσας 'if anywhere you heard' is a condition without κε. The speech closes here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply. τήν is 'her': what looks like the article is in Homer a pronoun. αὖ is 'in turn'. πεπνυμένος is the perfect participle of πέπνυμαι 'have one's wits about one', kept as 'prudent' every time it is used of Telemachus. ἀντίον is an adverb, 'face to face, in answer', and ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, μῆτερ, ἀληθείην καταλέξω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, mēter, alētheiēn katalexō.
sentences.l: “Therefore I to you, mother, the truth will recount.
sentences.i: “Then, mother, I will tell you the truth in full.
sentences.n: τοιγάρ is an inferential particle, 'therefore, well then'. ἀληθείην is the Ionic form of ἀλήθειαν, and καταλέξω is the future of καταλέγω 'recount, set out in full', the verb of recounting in full. Telemachus now begins his report; its two parts, Nestor and Menelaus, are told in this order.

sentences.t: ᾠχόμεθ’ ἔς τε Πύλον καὶ Νέστορα, ποιμένα λαῶν·
sentences.tr: ōichometh’ es te Pylon kai Nestora, poimena laōn·
sentences.l: We went both to Pylos and to Nestor, shepherd of the people;
sentences.i: We went to Pylos, to Nestor, shepherd of the people;
sentences.n: ᾠχόμεθ’ is ᾠχόμεθα, imperfect of οἴχομαι 'go, be gone'; the plural includes Telemachus's companions. ἔς is the Homeric spelling of εἰς. ποιμένα λαῶν is the standing 'shepherd of the people', accusative in apposition to Νέστορα; λαῶν is a genitive plural.

sentences.t:
δεξάμενος δέ με κεῖνος ἐν ὑψηλοῖσι δόμοισιν
ἐνδυκέως ἐφίλει, ὡς εἴ τε πατὴρ ἑὸν υἱὸν
ἐλθόντα χρόνιον νέον ἄλλοθεν·
sentences.tr:
dexamenos de me keinos en hypsēloisi domoisin
endykeōs ephilei, hōs ei te patēr heon huion
elthonta chronion neon allothen·
sentences.i: When he had received me in his high halls, he loved me kindly, as a father loves his own son who has come newly from elsewhere after a long time;
sentences.n: δεξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of δέχομαι 'receive'. κεῖνος is the Ionic form of ἐκεῖνος 'that man', here Nestor. ἐνδυκέως 'kindly' is kept in both layers. ὡς εἴ τε begins a comparison, 'as if'; ἑόν is the possessive 'his own' (not the relative), and the participle ἐλθόντα agrees with υἱόν. χρόνιον is 'after a long time', νέον 'newly', and ἄλλοθεν 'from elsewhere'. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐμὲ κεῖνος
ἐνδυκέως ἐκόμιζε σὺν υἱάσι κυδαλίμοισιν.
sentences.tr:
hōs eme keinos
endykeōs ekomize syn huiasi kydalimoisin.
sentences.l:
so me that man
kindly cared for, with his glorious sons.
sentences.i: so he cared for me kindly, together with his glorious sons.
sentences.n: ὣς ἐμὲ κεῖνος answers the comparison of the previous unit: 'so did that man (treat) me'. ἐκόμιζε is the imperfect of κομίζω 'care for'. υἱάσι is a dative plural of υἱός, 'with sons', and κυδαλίμοισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, 'glorious', an epithet that the poem also gives to Menelaus.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος οὔ ποτ’ ἔφασκεν,
ζωοῦ οὐδὲ θανόντος, ἐπιχθονίων τευ ἀκοῦσαι·
sentences.tr:
autar Odyssēos talasiphronos ou pot’ ephasken,
zōou oude thanontos, epichthoniōn teu akousai·
sentences.l:
but of enduring-minded Odysseus never did he say he had heard,
alive or dead, from any of men upon earth;
sentences.i: but of steadfast Odysseus, living or dead, he said he had never heard from any man on earth;
sentences.n: ταλασίφρων ('enduring-minded' in the first layer, 'steadfast' in the second) is one of three φρήν-epithets of Odysseus (with δαΐφρων and πολύφρων), always kept distinct. ἔφασκεν is an imperfect in -σκ-, 'he kept saying', with an infinitive ἀκοῦσαι 'to have heard' and οὔ ποτε 'never'. Ὀδυσσῆος is the genitive after ἀκοῦσαι 'hear of', ζωοῦ οὐδὲ θανόντος 'neither living nor dead' agrees with it, and τευ is τινος 'any'; ἐπιχθονίων 'men upon the earth' is a way of saying 'mortals'. The unit ends at an ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μ’ ἐς Ἀτρεΐδην, δουρικλειτὸν Μενέλαον,
ἵπποισι προὔπεμψε καὶ ἅρμασι κολλητοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
alla m’ es Atreïdēn, dourikleiton Menelaon,
hippoisi proupempse kai harmasi kollētoisin.
sentences.l:
but me to the son of Atreus, Menelaus famed-for-the-spear,
with horses he sent forward and a well-joined chariot.
sentences.i: but he sent me on, with horses and a well-joined chariot, to the son of Atreus, Menelaus, famed for his spear.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδην 'son of Atreus' is Menelaus, named in the apposition Μενέλαον, and δουρικλειτός 'famed for the spear' (from δόρυ and κλειτός) is his standing epithet. προὔπεμψε is the aorist of προπέμπω 'send forward', the augment run together with the preverb, and its subject is Nestor. ἵπποισι and ἅρμασι are datives of means; ἅρμα is a chariot, and the plural ἅρμασι is poetic for one vehicle. κολλητός 'glued, well-joined' describes its fitted frame.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἴδον Ἀργείην Ἑλένην, ἧς εἵνεκα πολλὰ
Ἀργεῖοι Τρῶές τε θεῶν ἰότητι μόγησαν.
sentences.tr:
enth’ idon Argeiēn Helenēn, hēs heineka polla
Argeioi Trōes te theōn iotēti mogēsan.
sentences.l:
There I saw Argive Helen, for whose sake many things
the Argives and the Trojans through the will of gods toiled.
sentences.i: There I saw Argive Helen, for whose sake the Argives and the Trojans toiled much by the will of the gods.
sentences.n: ἴδον is the aorist of ὁράω without augment. Ἀργείην is the Ionic feminine of Ἀργεῖος; Argive is here one of the poem's names for the Greeks at large, and Helen carries it as her own. ἧς εἵνεκα is 'for whose sake', εἵνεκα being the Homeric ἕνεκα. πολλά is the accusative of the thing undergone, 'many things', and μόγησαν is the aorist of μογέω 'toil'. θεῶν ἰότητι 'by the will of the gods' is an old phrase meaning favour or will. The second line of this unit is one that the Sirens also sing, in Book 12.

sentences.t:
εἴρετο δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
ὅττευ χρηΐζων ἱκόμην Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν·
sentences.tr:
eireto d’ autik’ epeita boēn agathos Menelaos
hotteu chrēïzōn hikomēn Lakedaimona dian·
sentences.l:
And he asked at once thereafter, good at the war-cry, Menelaus,
of what in need I came to heavenly Lacedaemon;
sentences.i: Then Menelaus, good at the war-cry, asked me at once what I wanted in coming to heavenly Lacedaemon;
sentences.n: εἴρετο is the imperfect middle of εἴρομαι 'ask', and βοὴν ἀγαθός 'good at the war-cry' is Menelaus's epithet, with βοήν an accusative of respect. ὅττευ is the Homeric genitive of ὅστις, 'for what', and χρηΐζων is the participle of χρηΐζω 'be in need of, want', so 'in need of what'. ἱκόμην is an aorist of ἱκνέομαι 'come', and Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν is the standing 'heavenly Lacedaemon'.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τῷ πᾶσαν ἀληθείην κατέλεξα·
sentences.tr: autar egō tōi pasan alētheiēn katelexa·
sentences.l: and I to him the whole truth recounted;
sentences.i: and I told him the whole truth;
sentences.n: κατέλεξα is the aorist of καταλέγω, the verb that Telemachus promised at 108, and ἀληθείην is the same noun, so that the promise is shown to be kept in the report itself. τῷ is a pronoun, 'to him'. πᾶσαν agrees with ἀληθείην, 'the whole truth'.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε δή με ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr: kai tote dē me epessin ameibomenos proseeipen·
sentences.l: and then indeed with words, answering me, he addressed me:
sentences.i: and then he answered me, and spoke:
sentences.n: ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν is a formula, 'answering with words, he addressed (me)'; ἔπεσσιν is a dative plural of ἔπος 'word', and με is 'me'. The line introduces what Menelaus said, which Telemachus now repeats to his mother. Menelaus's own words, inside Telemachus's speech, take single quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δὴ κρατερόφρονος ἀνδρὸς ἐν εὐνῇ
ἤθελον εὐνηθῆναι, ἀνάλκιδες αὐτοὶ ἐόντες.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, ē mala dē kraterophronos andros en eunēi
ēthelon eunēthēnai, analkides autoi eontes.
sentences.l:
“Ah! surely indeed in the bed of a strong-minded man
they wished to lie, themselves being men without might.
sentences.i: “Ah, they surely wished to lie in the bed of a mighty-minded man, weaklings that they themselves are!
sentences.n: Telemachus repeats what Menelaus said to him in Book 4 (4.333 ff.). ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of indignation. κρατερόφρονος is the genitive of κρατερόφρων, 'strong-minded' in the first layer and 'mighty-minded' in the second, and εὐνηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of εὐνάω, 'be laid to rest, lie down'. ἀνάλκιδες is 'without might, weak', and αὐτοί 'themselves'. The comparison that follows begins at 126.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὁπότ’ ἐν ξυλόχῳ ἔλαφος κρατεροῖο λέοντος
νεβροὺς κοιμήσασα νεηγενέας γαλαθηνοὺς
κνημοὺς ἐξερέῃσι καὶ ἄγκεα ποιήεντα
βοσκομένη,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hopot’ en xylochōi elaphos krateroio leontos
nebrous koimēsasa neēgeneas galathēnous
knēmous exereēisi kai ankea poiēenta
boskomenē,
sentences.l:
And as when, in the lair of a mighty lion, a hind,
her newborn, milk-fed fawns having lulled to rest,
ranges the wooded slopes and grassy glens,
grazing,
sentences.i: And as when a hind, having lulled her newborn, milk-fed fawns to rest in the lair of a mighty lion, ranges the wooded slopes and grassy glens as she grazes,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὁπότ’ 'and as when' opens a comparison, with ἔλαφος 'a hind' as its subject; ξύλοχος is a thicket or lair, and κρατεροῖο λέοντος 'of a mighty lion' is genitive. κοιμήσασα is the aorist participle of κοιμάω 'lull to sleep'; νεβρούς are 'fawns', νεηγενέας 'newborn' and γαλαθηνούς 'at the milk'. ἐξερέῃσι is a subjunctive of ἐξερέω 'search out, range over', with κνημούς 'wooded slopes' and ἄγκεα 'glens' as its objects, and βοσκομένη is a middle participle, 'grazing'. The comparison is finished in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα ἑὴν εἰσήλυθεν εὐνήν,
ἀμφοτέροισι δὲ τοῖσιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐφῆκεν,
ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς κείνοισιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐφήσει.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epeita heēn eisēlythen eunēn,
amphoteroisi de toisin aeikea potmon ephēken,
hōs Odyseus keinoisin aeikea potmon ephēsei.
sentences.i: but the lion then came back to his own lair, and sent an unseemly doom upon them both; so will Odysseus send an unseemly doom upon those men.
sentences.n: The lion of the simile returns to his lair and sends a doom upon both fawn and doe; the phrase ἀεικέα πότμον 'an unseemly doom' stands in both lines, so that the second applies the picture to the suitors. ἐφῆκεν is the aorist of ἐφίημι 'send upon', ἐφήσει its future, and ὣς 'so' begins the comparison's application. Odysseus is named without an epithet; κείνοισιν is 'upon those men', the suitors.

sentences.t:
αἲ γάρ, Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον,
τοῖος ἐὼν οἷός ποτ’ ἐϋκτιμένῃ ἐνὶ Λέσβῳ
ἐξ ἔριδος Φιλομηλεΐδῃ ἐπάλαισεν ἀναστάς,
κὰδ δ’ ἔβαλε κρατερῶς, κεχάροντο δὲ πάντες Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.tr:
ai gar, Zeu te pater kai Athēnaiē kai Apollon,
toios eōn hoios pot’ eÿktimenēi eni Lesbōi
ex eridos Philomēleïdēi epalaisen anastas,
kad d’ ebale kraterōs, kecharonto de pantes Achaioi,
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
such as he was, when once in well-built Lesbos,
rising up from a quarrel, he wrestled against Philomeleides,
and threw him down mightily, and all the Achaeans rejoiced —
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — Odysseus were such as he was when once, in well-built Lesbos, he rose up from a quarrel and wrestled Philomeleides, and threw him down hard, to the joy of all the Achaeans —
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ introduces a wish, 'would that', which Menelaus makes to Father Zeus, Athena and Apollo. τοῖος ἐών ... οἷος ποτε is 'being such as once': Odysseus is imagined as he was once in Lesbos. Φιλομηλεΐδῃ is a patronymic of an unknown Philomeles, the opponent in the wrestling bout, and ἐπάλαισεν is the aorist of παλαίω 'wrestle'. κὰδ δ’ ἔβαλε is tmesis for κατέβαλε, 'threw him down'. The wish is completed in the next unit.

sentences.t: τοῖος ἐὼν μνηστῆρσιν ὁμιλήσειεν Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: toios eōn mnēstērsin homilēseien Odysseus·
sentences.l: being such, may Odysseus come among the suitors;
sentences.i: then, being such a man, Odysseus might come among the suitors!
sentences.n: τοῖος ἐὼν answers the earlier τοῖος ἐὼν οἷος, 'such as he was then, may he be now'. μνηστῆρσιν is a dative plural with ὁμιλήσειεν, 'consort with', 'come among', an optative of wish in the aorist. The line also stands in Book 1 (1.265).

sentences.t: πάντες κ’ ὠκύμοροί τε γενοίατο πικρόγαμοί τε.
sentences.tr: pantes k’ ōkymoroi te genoiato pikrogamoi te.
sentences.l: all of them would become swift-doomed and bitter-wedded.
sentences.i: All of them would meet a swift doom and a bitter marriage.
sentences.n: πάντες κ’ ὠκύμοροί τε γενοίατο πικρόγαμοί τε is the result: κε with the optative says 'they would become'. ὠκύμορος 'swift-doomed' and πικρόγαμος 'bitter-wedded' are compounds, the first 'with a swift doom' and the second 'with a bitter marriage'; the first is built on μόρος 'doom' and ὠκύς 'swift', the second on γάμος 'marriage' and πικρός 'bitter'.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δ’ ἅ μ’ εἰρωτᾷς καὶ λίσσεαι, οὐκ ἂν ἐγώ γε
ἄλλα παρὲξ εἴποιμι παρακλιδὸν οὐδ’ ἀπατήσω,
ἀλλὰ τὰ μέν μοι ἔειπε γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής,
τῶν οὐδέν τοι ἐγὼ κρύψω ἔπος οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω.
sentences.tr:
tauta d’ ha m’ eirōtāis kai lisseai, ouk an egō ge
alla parex eipoimi paraklidon oud’ apatēsō,
alla ta men moi eeipe gerōn halios nēmertēs,
tōn ouden toi egō krypsō epos oud’ epikeusō.
sentences.l:
But these things which you ask me and beg of me, I myself
would not say otherwise, in a roundabout way, nor will I deceive you;
but what the unerring old man of the sea told me,
of that I will hide from you no word, nor keep anything back.
sentences.i: But as for these things you ask and beg of me, I for my part will not speak beside the point, evasively, nor will I deceive you; rather, what the unerring old man of the sea told me — of that I will hide no word from you, nor keep anything back.
sentences.n: Menelaus passes to the answer to Telemachus's question. ἅ μ’ εἰρωτᾷς καὶ λίσσεαι: 'what you ask me and beg of me'. παρὲξ εἴποιμι 'say beside the point' and παρακλιδόν 'evasively, sideways' describe what he will not do. γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής is the standing 'unerring old man of the sea', the sea-god Proteus of Book 4; νημερτής 'unerring' is a standing word for his speech. ἐπικεύσω is the aorist subjunctive of ἐπικεύθω 'hide'.

sentences.t:
φῆ μιν ὅ γ’ ἐν νήσῳ ἰδέειν κρατέρ’ ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα,
νύμφης ἐν μεγάροισι Καλυψοῦς, ἥ μιν ἀνάγκῃ
ἴσχει·
sentences.tr:
phē min ho g’ en nēsōi ideein krater’ alge’ echonta,
nymphēs en megaroisi Kalypsous, hē min anankēi
ischei·
sentences.i: He said that he had seen him on an island, beset by harsh pains, in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him there against his will;
sentences.n: φῆ is the imperfect of φημί, 'he said', and its subject ὅ γ’ is Proteus, the old man of the previous unit. μιν 'him' is Odysseus, the object of ἰδέειν, an aorist infinitive of εἶδον 'see'. κρατέρ’ ἄλγε’ is κρατερὰ ἄλγεα, 'harsh pains', with ἔχοντα 'having, being beset by'. ἀνάγκῃ is a dative of manner, 'by constraint'. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ οὐ δύναται ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.tr: ho d’ ou dynatai hēn patrida gaian hikesthai.
sentences.l: but he is not able his own fatherland to reach;
sentences.i: and he cannot reach his own native land;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ is 'but he', Odysseus. ἣν is the possessive ὅς, 'his own', not the relative: ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'his own fatherland', the standing phrase. ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι 'reach'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ οἱ πάρα νῆες ἐπήρετμοι καὶ ἑταῖροι,
οἵ κέν μιν πέμποιεν ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
ou gar hoi para nēes epēretmoi kai hetairoi,
hoi ken min pempoien ep’ eurea nōta thalassēs.
sentences.l:
For he has no oared ships nor companions,
who might send him over the broad back of the sea.
sentences.i: for he has no oared ships or companions who might convey him over the sea's broad back.
sentences.n: These two lines are those that Proteus used in Book 4. ἐπήρετμοι is 'fitted with oars'; πάρα is πάρεστι 'are at hand', with οἱ 'to him'. κέν with the optative μιν πέμποιεν is a clause of characteristic, 'such as might convey him'. Line 146 has no punctuation in Murray's text; the unit ends there because a new paragraph opens at 147. The single quotation mark closes Menelaus's speech here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀτρεΐδης, δουρικλειτὸς Μενέλαος.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ Atreïdēs, dourikleitos Menelaos.
sentences.l: So spoke the son of Atreus, Menelaus famed-for-the-spear.
sentences.i: So spoke the son of Atreus, Menelaus, famed for his spear.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης 'son of Atreus' is Menelaus, named in the apposition Μενέλαος, as Ἀτρεΐδην is at 116, and ὣς ἔφατ’ is a closing formula, 'so spoke', naming the speaker. Menelaus's words, quoted inside Telemachus's speech, are finished, and Telemachus's own report resumes in the next unit.

sentences.t: ταῦτα τελευτήσας νεόμην·
sentences.tr: tauta teleutēsas neomēn·
sentences.l: Having brought these things to an end, I set out for home;
sentences.i: When I had finished all this, I set out for home;
sentences.n: τελευτήσας is the aorist participle of τελευτάω 'bring to an end', and νεόμην the imperfect of νέομαι 'go home', with inceptive force, 'I set out for home'. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἔδοσαν δέ μοι οὖρον
ἀθάνατοι, τοί μ’ ὦκα φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἔπεμψαν.
sentences.tr:
edosan de moi ouron
athanatoi, toi m’ ōka philēn es patrid’ epempsan.
sentences.l:
and gave me a fair-wind
the immortals, who quickly to my dear fatherland sent me.”
sentences.i: and the immortal gods gave me a fair wind and sent me quickly to my own dear fatherland.”
sentences.n: οὖρον 'a fair wind' is the object of ἔδοσαν, whose subject ἀθάνατοι 'the immortals' stands in the next line. τοί is a relative here, 'who', and μ’ is με. The speech of Telemachus ends here, with the closing mark.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῇ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε.
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tēi d’ ara thymon eni stēthessin orine.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the heart in her breast he stirred.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he stirred the heart in her breast.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the standing closing phrase 'so he spoke'. τῇ is a dative of interest, 'in her', and θυμὸν ... ὄρινε, 'stirred her heart', has ὄρινε as a past tense of ὀρίνω 'stir, rouse', without the augment. στήθεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε Θεοκλύμενος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipe Theoklymenos theoeidēs·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also Theoclymenus, godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: And Theoclymenus, godlike in form, spoke up among them as well:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is 'among them' with μετέειπε 'spoke among', and καί 'also' marks Theoclymenus as a further speaker. Θεοκλύμενος is the seer who, as 160–161 show, sailed on Telemachus's ship, and θεοειδής 'godlike in form' is his epithet here, kept in the house rendering.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι αἰδοίη Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος,
ἦ τοι ὅ γ’ οὐ σάφα οἶδεν, ἐμεῖο δὲ σύνθεο μῦθον·
sentences.tr:
ō gynai aidoiē Laertiadeō Odysēos,
ē toi ho g’ ou sapha oiden, emeio de syntheo mython·
sentences.l:
“O wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, revered one,
he in truth does not clearly know; but of me take in the word;
sentences.i: “Revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, he does not in fact know clearly; but take my word to heart;
sentences.n: γύναι is a vocative, and αἰδοίη 'revered' agrees with it; Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος 'of Odysseus, Laertes' son' is a genitive in -εω, the Ionic form, depending on γύναι as the wife of. ὅ γ’ is Telemachus: Theoclymenus says that he does not clearly know. σύνθεο is the aorist imperative middle of συντίθημι 'put together, take in'. ἐμεῖο is an old genitive of ἐγώ, 'my', going with μῦθον, the object. The unit ends at an ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀτρεκέως γάρ σοι μαντεύσομαι οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω·
sentences.tr: atrekeōs gar soi manteusomai oud’ epikeusō·
sentences.l: for exactly to you I will prophesy, nor will I keep anything back;
sentences.i: for I will prophesy to you exactly, and will keep nothing back;
sentences.n: ἀτρεκέως 'exactly' is an adverb. μαντεύσομαι is the future of μαντεύομαι 'prophesy, speak as a seer'. οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω is an aorist subjunctive used as a future, 'nor will I keep anything back', as in the same formula at 141.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν Ζεὺς πρῶτα θεῶν, ξενίη τε τράπεζα
ἱστίη τ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος, ἣν ἀφικάνω,
sentences.tr:
istō nyn Zeus prōta theōn, xeniē te trapeza
histiē t’ Odysēos amymonos, hēn aphikanō,
sentences.l:
Let Zeus now know, first of the gods, and the table of hospitality,
and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come;
sentences.i: Let Zeus now know, first of the gods, and the table of hospitality, and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come;
sentences.n: ἴστω is the third person imperative of οἶδα, 'let him know'; the oath calls on Zeus, the table of hospitality and the hearth of Odysseus. ξενίη τε τράπεζα is the 'table of hospitality', a way of calling on the hospitality which the table represents; ἱστίη is the Ionic form of ἑστία 'hearth'. ἀμύμονος 'blameless' is the standing epithet of Odysseus here, and ἣν ἀφικάνω is a relative clause, 'to which I have come'. The oath continues in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἦ τοι Ὀδυσεὺς ἤδη ἐν πατρίδι γαίῃ,
ἥμενος ἢ ἕρπων, τάδε πευθόμενος κακὰ ἔργα,
ἔστιν, ἀτὰρ μνηστῆρσι κακὸν πάντεσσι φυτεύει·
sentences.tr:
hōs ē toi Odyseus ēdē en patridi gaiēi,
hēmenos ē herpōn, tade peuthomenos kaka erga,
estin, atar mnēstērsi kakon pantessi phyteuei·
sentences.i: that Odysseus is already in his fatherland, whether sitting or creeping about, learning of these evil deeds, and is devising evil for all the suitors;
sentences.n: The ὡς clause gives the content of the oath, 'that'; ἦ τοι is 'truly'. ἔστιν at the start of the last line completes it: 'is (there)'. ἥμενος ἢ ἕρπων 'sitting or creeping' means that wherever he is and whatever he does, he is already in the country, with ἕρπω 'creep, go slowly'. πευθόμενος is the present participle of πεύθομαι 'learn', and φυτεύει 'plants' is kept literal in the first layer; the second layer says 'devising', as for κακὰ φύτευεν elsewhere.

sentences.t:
τοῖον ἐγὼν οἰωνὸν ἐϋσσέλμου ἐπὶ νηὸς
ἥμενος ἐφρασάμην καὶ Τηλεμάχῳ ἐγεγώνευν.
sentences.tr:
toion egōn oiōnon eÿsselmou epi nēos
hēmenos ephrasamēn kai Tēlemachōi egegōneun.
sentences.l:
such a bird of omen I, upon the well-benched ship
sitting, observed, and to Telemachus I called out.”
sentences.i: I saw such a bird of omen as I sat on the well-benched ship, and I called out to Telemachus.”
sentences.n: τοῖον οἰωνόν 'such a bird of omen' is the sign Theoclymenus saw from the ship; the Greek does not describe it here. ἐϋσσέλμου is the genitive of ἐΰσσελμος 'well-benched', an epithet of ships. ἐφρασάμην is the aorist middle of φράζομαι 'observe, notice', and ἐγεγώνευν the imperfect of γεγωνέω 'call out, shout so as to be heard', with Τηλεμάχῳ in the dative. The speech closes here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The reply formula with αὖτε 'in turn' and προσέειπε 'addressed'. τόν is 'him', Theoclymenus. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια is Penelope's epithet, kept as 'circumspect' every time; it is not the same as the epithet that means 'sound-minded'.

sentences.t: αἲ γὰρ τοῦτο, ξεῖνε, ἔπος τετελεσμένον εἴη·
sentences.tr: ai gar touto, xeine, epos tetelesmenon eiē·
sentences.l: “Would that this, stranger, word fulfilled might be;
sentences.i: “If only this word of yours, stranger, might be fulfilled;
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ begins a wish, as at 132, and εἴη completes it as an optative of wish: 'would that this word might be fulfilled'. ξεῖνε is the vocative 'stranger'. τετελεσμένον is the perfect passive participle of τελέω 'fulfil', agreeing with ἔπος 'word'.

sentences.t:
τῷ κε τάχα γνοίης φιλότητά τε πολλά τε δῶρα
ἐξ ἐμεῦ, ὡς ἄν τίς σε συναντόμενος μακαρίζοι.
sentences.tr:
tōi ke tacha gnoiēs philotēta te polla te dōra
ex emeu, hōs an tis se synantomenos makarizoi.
sentences.l:
then soon you would know friendship and many gifts
from me, so that someone meeting you would call you blessed.”
sentences.i: Then you would soon know friendship from me, and many gifts, so that anyone who met you would call you blessed.”
sentences.n: τῷ is 'then, in that case'. γνοίης is a potential optative of γιγνώσκω 'know'; with κε it says 'you would know'. φιλότητά τε πολλά τε δῶρα is 'friendship and many gifts'. ὡς ἄν with the optative μακαρίζοι gives a purpose clause, 'so that one meeting you would call you blessed'; the speech of Penelope ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
μνηστῆρες δὲ πάροιθεν Ὀδυσσῆος μεγάροιο
δίσκοισιν τέρποντο καὶ αἰγανέῃσιν ἱέντες,
ἐν τυκτῷ δαπέδῳ, ὅθι περ πάρος ὕβριν ἔχοντες.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
mnēstēres de paroithen Odyssēos megaroio
diskoisin terponto kai aiganeēisin hientes,
en tyktōi dapedōi, hothi per paros hybrin echontes.
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
but the suitors, in front of the hall of Odysseus,
with discuses were taking delight, and with javelins throwing,
on the smoothed pavement, where indeed before, holding their insolence.
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, while the suitors, in front of Odysseus's hall, were amusing themselves throwing the discus and the javelin on the levelled floor, where they had played before, indulging their insolence.
sentences.n: The scene changes from the hall to the courtyard, where the suitors are. τοιαῦτα is 'such things', and πρὸς ἀλλήλους 'to one another'. δίσκοισιν and αἰγανέῃσιν are datives of means, with the participle ἱέντες 'throwing'. τυκτῷ δαπέδῳ is 'the levelled floor', a dative of place. ὅθι περ πάρος: 'where indeed before', the place where they had played before; ὕβριν ἔχοντες 'holding their insolence' repeats the poem's word for what they do.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ δείπνηστος ἔην καὶ ἐπήλυθε μῆλα
πάντοθεν ἐξ ἀγρῶν, οἱ δ’ ἤγαγον οἳ τὸ πάρος περ,
καὶ τότε δή σφιν ἔειπε Μέδων·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē deipnēstos eēn kai epēlythe mēla
pantothen ex agrōn, hoi d’ ēgagon hoi to paros per,
kai tote dē sphin eeipe Medōn·
sentences.i: But when it was time for the meal, and the flocks had come up from every side from the farms, driven by the men who had done so before, then Medon spoke to them:
sentences.n: δείπνηστος is 'time for the meal', from δεῖπνον. ἐπήλυθε is the aorist of ἐπέρχομαι, with the neuter plural subject μῆλα 'flocks' (sheep and goats) taking a singular verb. The relative οἳ τὸ πάρος περ is 'who did so before', the men who always drove them. σφιν is the pronoun 'to them', and ἔειπε is Homer's form of εἶπε 'said'. Μέδων is the herald of the next unit. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὃς γάρ ῥα μάλιστα
ἥνδανε κηρύκων, καί σφιν παρεγίγνετο δαιτί·
sentences.tr:
hos gar rha malista
hēndane kērykōn, kai sphin paregigneto daiti·
sentences.l:
who most of the heralds
pleased, and was with them at the feast:
sentences.i: for he was the one of the heralds who pleased them best, and he was with them at the meal:
sentences.n: ὃς γάρ ῥα explains why Medon is the speaker, 'for he'; ῥα is the epic particle ῥά 'then, indeed'. μάλιστα ... κηρύκων 'most of the heralds'. ἥνδανε is the imperfect of ἁνδάνω 'please', with the augment (ἐ + ἁ) run into ἥ, and παρεγίγνετο is the imperfect of παραγίγνομαι 'be present'. δαιτί is a dative of place, 'at the feast'. The unit ends at an ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κοῦροι, ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντες ἐτέρφθητε φρέν’ ἀέθλοις,
ἔρχεσθε πρὸς δώμαθ’, ἵν’ ἐντυνώμεθα δαῖτα·
sentences.tr:
kouroi, epei dē pantes eterphthēte phren’ aethlois,
erchesthe pros dōmath’, hin’ entynōmetha daita·
sentences.l:
“Young men, since all of you have taken your pleasure in the contests,
go to the house, that we may make ready the feast;
sentences.i: “Young men, since you have all had your pleasure in the contests, go to the house, so that we may prepare the meal;
sentences.n: κοῦροι is a vocative plural, 'young men'. ἐτέρφθητε is the aorist passive of τέρπω 'delight', with φρέν’ (φρένα) as an accusative of respect, 'in mind'. ἀέθλοις is a dative plural of ἄεθλον 'contest'. ἔρχεσθε is an imperative, and ἵν’ ἐντυνώμεθα, a purpose clause with the subjunctive, means 'that we may make ready'; δαῖτα is 'the feast'.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι χέρειον ἐν ὥρῃ δεῖπνον ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti chereion en hōrēi deipnon helesthai.
sentences.l: for it is not at all worse in season a meal to take.”
sentences.i: for it is no worse to take one's meal at the proper time.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι χέρειον is 'for it is in no way worse', and ἐν ὥρῃ 'in season, at the right time'. δεῖπνον ἑλέσθαι is 'to take a meal', with ἑλέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of αἱρέω. The herald's speech closes with a common-sense saying.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἀνστάντες ἔβαν πείθοντό τε μύθῳ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ anstantes eban peithonto te mythōi.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they, rising up, went and obeyed his word.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they rose and went, obeying his word.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is 'so he spoke', ἔφαθ’ being ἔφατο with its vowel elided. ἀνστάντες is the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, 'having risen'. ἔβαν is a form of ἔβησαν, 'they went', and πείθοντο is the imperfect middle of πείθομαι 'obey'; μύθῳ is a dative, 'his word'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἵκοντο δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας,
χλαίνας μὲν κατέθεντο κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε,
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ hikonto domous eu naietaontas,
chlainas men katethento kata klismous te thronous te,
sentences.l:
But when they reached the well-inhabited house,
cloaks, on the one hand, they laid down on seats and chairs,
sentences.i: When they reached the well-inhabited house, they laid their cloaks down on seats and chairs,
sentences.n: δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας 'the well-inhabited house' is a plural for one dwelling. ἵκοντο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι 'reach', and κατέθεντο the aorist middle of κατατίθημι 'lay down'; μέν ... is answered by οἱ δέ in the next unit. κλισμούς and θρόνους are two kinds of seat, the first a reclining seat and the second a chair.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἱέρευον ὄϊς μεγάλους καὶ πίονας αἶγας,
ἵρευον δὲ σύας σιάλους καὶ βοῦν ἀγελαίην,
δαῖτ’ ἐντυνόμενοι.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hiereuon oïs megalous kai pionas aigas,
hireuon de syas sialous kai boun agelaiēn,
dait’ entynomenoi.
sentences.l:
and they were sacrificing great sheep and fat goats,
and were sacrificing fat swine and a cow of the herd,
making ready the feast.
sentences.i: while others slaughtered large sheep and fat goats, and slaughtered fat swine and a cow from the herd, preparing the meal.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ 'and they' answers the μέν of the previous unit. ἱέρευον and ἵρευον are two forms of the imperfect of ἱερεύω, 'slaughter for sacrifice', and the meat is for the feast. ὄϊς is an accusative plural of ὄϊς 'sheep', and πίονας 'fat' agrees with αἶγας. σύας σιάλους is 'fat swine'. βοῦν ἀγελαίην is 'a cow of the herd'. ἐντυνόμενοι is the present participle middle of ἐντύνω 'make ready'. The unit ends at a full stop in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἐξ ἀγροῖο πόλινδε
ὠτρύνοντ’ Ὀδυσεύς τ’ ἰέναι καὶ δῖος ὑφορβός.
sentences.tr:
toi d’ ex agroio polinde
ōtrynont’ Odyseus t’ ienai kai dios hyphorbos.
sentences.l:
And they from the farm to the town
were hastening to go, Odysseus and the heavenly swineherd.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Odysseus and the heavenly swineherd were hastening to set out from the farm for the town.
sentences.n: τοὶ is the pronoun 'they', the old τοί for οἱ, pointing to the pair named at the end of the next line. ἐξ ἀγροῖο is 'from the farm', the genitive in -οιο. πόλινδε is πόλιν with the suffix -δε 'toward', 'to the town'. ὠτρύνοντ’ is ὠτρύνοντο, imperfect middle of ὀτρύνω, 'were urging themselves on, hurried', with the infinitive ἰέναι. Odysseus is named and δῖος ὑφορβός 'the heavenly swineherd' is Eumaeus.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε συβώτης, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche sybōtēs, orchamos andrōn·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning the swineherd, chief of men:
sentences.i: The swineherd, chief of men, was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is 'among them', and μύθων ἦρχε is 'began the speeches', a standing way of saying that someone speaks first. συβώτης is 'swineherd', and ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν 'chief of men' is an honorific for him, kept in the house rendering. This is Eumaeus, whom the Greek names only at 199; ὑφορβός and συβώτης are both 'swineherd'.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἐπεὶ ἂρ δὴ ἔπειτα πόλινδ’ ἰέναι μενεαίνεις
σήμερον, ὡς ἐπέτελλεν ἄναξ ἐμός—ἦ σ’ ἂν ἐγώ γε
αὐτοῦ βουλοίμην σταθμῶν ῥυτῆρα λιπέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
xein’, epei ar dē epeita polind’ ienai meneaineis
sēmeron, hōs epetellen anax emos—ē s’ an egō ge
autou bouloimēn stathmōn rhytēra lipesthai·
sentences.i: “Stranger, since you are eager to go to the town today, as my lord ordered — for my own part I would rather you were left here as the protector of the steading;
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ is the vocative of ξεῖνος 'stranger'. μενεαίνεις is a present of μενεαίνω 'be eager, strive'. ἐπέτελλεν is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω 'order'. ἄναξ ἐμός 'my lord' is Telemachus, who gave the order in the previous part. The words between the dashes are a parenthesis: ἦ σ’ ἂν ἐγώ γε ... βουλοίμην 'truly I for my part would wish', with σ’ = σε 'you' as the subject of the infinitive λιπέσθαι 'to be left', the aorist middle of λείπω in a passive sense. ῥυτῆρα is 'protector, defender', and σταθμῶν is a plural for the one steading. The unit ends at an ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὸν αἰδέομαι καὶ δείδια, μή μοι ὀπίσσω
νεικείῃ·
sentences.tr:
alla ton aideomai kai deidia, mē moi opissō
neikeiēi·
sentences.l:
but him I revere and fear, lest afterwards
he rebuke me;
sentences.i: but I stand in awe of him and fear that he will rebuke me afterwards;
sentences.n: τόν is 'him', the lord of the previous unit. αἰδέομαι and δείδια are two verbs of respect and fear, 'I revere' and 'I am afraid', the second a perfect used as a present and followed by μή 'lest'. νεικείῃ is the subjunctive of νεικέω 'quarrel with, rebuke', in the Ionic spelling. ὀπίσσω is 'afterwards'. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
χαλεπαὶ δέ τ’ ἀνάκτων εἰσὶν ὁμοκλαί—
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἴομεν·
sentences.tr:
chalepai de t’ anaktōn eisin homoklai—
all’ age nyn iomen·
sentences.l:
hard are the rebukes of lords —
but come, now let us go;
sentences.i: a lord's rebukes are hard to bear — but come, let us go now;
sentences.n: χαλεπαὶ ... ὁμοκλαί is 'harsh rebukes', and ἀνάκτων is the genitive plural of ἄναξ, 'of lords'. δέ τε marks a general truth. The second dash closes the parenthesis that opened at 186, and ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἴομεν is the main clause that ἐπεί at 185 was waiting for. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come', and νῦν ἴομεν a hortatory subjunctive of εἶμι 'go', a short-vowel subjunctive. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
δὴ γὰρ μέμβλωκε μάλιστα
ἦμαρ, ἀτὰρ τάχα τοι ποτὶ ἕσπερα ῥίγιον ἔσται.
sentences.tr:
dē gar memblōke malista
ēmar, atar tacha toi poti hespera rhigion estai.
sentences.l:
for indeed it has gone far, the greater part of
the day, and soon toward evening it will be colder.”
sentences.i: for the day is already far spent, and soon, toward evening, it will be colder.”
sentences.n: μέμβλωκε is the perfect of βλώσκω 'go' (aorist μολεῖν), and with ἦμαρ 'day' it means 'has gone far', 'is far advanced'. μάλιστα is 'chiefly, to a great degree'. τάχα is 'soon', and ποτὶ ἕσπερα is 'toward evening', with ποτί the Homeric form of πρός. ῥίγιον is the comparative of ῥῖγος 'cold', 'it will be more chilling'; ἔσται is impersonal, 'it will be'. τοι is either 'for you' or the particle 'indeed'; it is left unrendered. Eumaeus's speech closes here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply: ἀπαμειβόμενος is 'answering', and προσέφη 'addressed', so that the line says 'answering, he addressed'. πολύμητις 'of many wiles' is the standing epithet of Odysseus; μῆτις is cunning or counsel. The speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t: γιγνώσκω, φρονέω·
sentences.tr: gignōskō, phroneō·
sentences.l: “I know it, I understand;
sentences.i: “I see, I understand;
sentences.n: γιγνώσκω and φρονέω are two verbs for the one idea, 'I have it'. The first is 'I recognise', the second 'I am aware, I take your point'. Odysseus replies to Eumaeus's fear by showing that he has understood it. The unit ends at an ano teleia.

sentences.t: τά γε δὴ νοέοντι κελεύεις.
sentences.tr: ta ge dē noeonti keleueis.
sentences.l: these things, indeed, to one who perceives you bid.
sentences.i: you are giving these instructions to a man who understands.
sentences.n: τά γε 'these things' is the object of κελεύεις 'you bid'. νοέοντι is the dative masculine participle of νοέω 'perceive', agreeing with the unstated 'to a man who understands'. The whole line is also 16.136, where Eumaeus says it to Telemachus.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν, σὺ δ’ ἔπειτα διαμπερὲς ἡγεμόνευε.
sentences.tr: all’ iomen, sy d’ epeita diamperes hēgemoneue.
sentences.l: But let us go, and you then right through lead the way.
sentences.i: But let us go, and you lead the way, right through.
sentences.n: ἴομεν is the same hortatory subjunctive as at 190, and ἡγεμόνευε is the present imperative of ἡγεμονεύω 'lead'. διαμπερές is an adverb, 'right through, continuously', of the whole way. σύ δ’ ἔπειτα is 'and you then', taking up what Eumaeus ought to do.

sentences.t:
δὸς δέ μοι, εἴ ποθί τοι ῥόπαλον τετμημένον ἐστίν,
σκηρίπτεσθ’, ἐπεὶ ἦ φατ’ ἀρισφαλέ’ ἔμμεναι οὐδόν.
sentences.tr:
dos de moi, ei pothi toi rhopalon tetmēmenon estin,
skēriptesth’, epei ē phat’ arisphale’ emmenai oudon.
sentences.l:
and give me, if anywhere you have a club cut,
to lean on, since indeed you say the threshold is very slippery.”
sentences.i: and give me, if you have a club cut anywhere, to lean on, since you say the ground is very slippery.”
sentences.n: δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι. ῥόπαλον is a heavy stick, 'club' as at 9.319 (the Cyclops's), here a rough walking-stick, the same thing that is called a σκῆπτρον 'staff' at 199. τετμημένον is the perfect passive participle of τέμνω 'cut'. σκηρίπτεσθ’ is a present infinitive of purpose, 'to prop oneself'; ἐπεί is 'since'. ἦ φατ’ is φατε 'you say', a plural of general address that the Greek does not name; ἀρισφαλέ’ is ἀρισφαλέα, 'very slippery', agreeing with οὐδόν. οὐδός is 'threshold', here probably the ground underfoot on the way.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἀεικέα βάλλετο πήρην,
πυκνὰ ῥωγαλέην·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai amph’ ōmoisin aeikea balleto pērēn,
pykna rhōgaleēn·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and about his shoulders an unseemly wallet he threw,
thickly torn;
sentences.i: So he said, and slung an unseemly wallet about his shoulders, torn in many places;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί is a formula, 'he spoke, and', with ἦ from ἠμί 'say' and ῥα the particle. βάλλετο is the imperfect middle of βάλλω, 'threw about himself'. πήρην 'wallet' is the beggar's bag, ἀεικέα 'unseemly' and ῥωγαλέην 'torn' its two adjectives, and πυκνά an adverb 'thickly, in many places'. This is the wallet Athena gave him in Book 13 (13.437–438). The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ στρόφος ἦεν ἀορτήρ·
sentences.tr: en de strophos ēen aortēr·
sentences.l: and on it a twisted cord was, for a strap.
sentences.i: and on it was a twisted cord to serve as a strap.
sentences.n: ἐν δέ is the adverb 'and on it', pointing to the wallet. στρόφος 'twisted cord' and ἀορτήρ 'strap' stand side by side, the cord being the strap. ἦεν is Homer's ἦν 'was'. The line is also in Book 13 (13.438).

sentences.t: Εὔμαιος δ’ ἄρα οἱ σκῆπτρον θυμαρὲς ἔδωκε.
sentences.tr: Eumaios d’ ara hoi skēptron thymares edōke.
sentences.l: and Eumaeus then to him a heart-fitting staff gave.
sentences.i: and Eumaeus gave him a staff that suited him.
sentences.n: Εὔμαιος is named here for the first time in this part and is the swineherd. σκῆπτρον is 'staff', the object that Odysseus asked for as ῥόπαλον. θυμαρές is 'fitting the heart, to his liking', neuter agreeing with σκῆπτρον. ἔδωκε is the aorist of δίδωμι, and ἄρα οἱ are the particle 'then' and 'to him'.

sentences.t:
τὼ βήτην, σταθμὸν δὲ κύνες καὶ βώτορες ἄνδρες
ῥύατ’ ὄπισθε μένοντες·
sentences.tr:
tō bētēn, stathmon de kynes kai bōtores andres
rhyat’ opisthe menontes·
sentences.l:
The two went; and the steading the dogs and the herdsmen
guarded, staying behind;
sentences.i: The two went on their way, while the dogs and the herdsmen stayed behind and guarded the steading;
sentences.n: τὼ βήτην is a dual, 'the two went', with βήτην the aorist dual of βαίνω. σταθμόν is the steading, the object of ῥύατ’ (= ῥύατο, an old 3 pl. in -ατο, the sense of ῥύοντο), 'were guarding'. κύνες καὶ βώτορες ἄνδρες 'the dogs and the herding men' says the farm was left in the care of those who stay; ὄπισθε μένοντες 'staying behind' goes with ῥύατ’. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐς πόλιν ἦγεν ἄνακτα
πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ἐναλίγκιον ἠδὲ γέροντι,
σκηπτόμενον·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ es polin ēgen anakta
ptōchōi leugaleōi enalinkion ēde geronti,
skēptomenon·
sentences.i: and the swineherd led his lord to the town, looking like a pitiful beggar and an old man, leaning on his staff;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is 'and he', the swineherd, and ἄνακτα 'his lord' is the poet's word for Odysseus, though Eumaeus does not know who the beggar is. πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ἐναλίγκιον ἠδὲ γέροντι is 'like a pitiful beggar and an old man', in the dative after ἐναλίγκιον. σκηπτόμενον is the participle of σκήπτομαι 'lean on a staff', and agrees with ἄνακτα. The unit ends at an ano teleia.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ λυγρὰ περὶ χροῒ εἵματα ἕστο.
sentences.tr: ta de lygra peri chroï heimata hesto.
sentences.l: and the grievous clothes about his skin he was wearing.
sentences.i: and he was clothed in those grievous clothes about his body.
sentences.n: τὰ δέ is the pronoun, 'and those', with λυγρά 'grievous' and εἵματα 'clothes'. χροῒ is a dative of χρώς 'skin, body', and ἕστο is the pluperfect middle of ἕννυμι, 'had put on, was clothed in'.
